title: Shooting victim was mentally ill Neighbour; Woman's 911 call summoned police on Saturday Man was killed after he wounded officer with shotgun blast
article: A woman who called 911 about the man shot to death by police on the weekend said she could tell he was mentally ill and needed help.
While criticizing what she called media sensationalism over the shooting, Tanya Harris praised police behaviour before and after the tragedy as "exemplary."
When Antonio Bellon loudly knocked on her front door Saturday afternoon, Harris could tell "he was a sick man. You could see the rage in his face, the eyes and so on."
Harris is the director of Shiatsu Therapy Clinic on Dufferin St., next door to where Bellon, 63, was shot dead by a police officer after wounding Sergeant Allan Jenkins with a shotgun blast.
Harris, who moved her storefront clinic into the area six months ago, barely knew Bellon, who lived in the house next door. But when she saw him that day, she could sense his pent-up rage.

She said after she called police she asked them "to be very gentle with him and tell him this place has patients coming in and out and it's just not proper to be, you know, banging on neighbours' doors and so on."
She offered her condolences to Bellon's family and emphasized that the Rogers Rd. and Dufferin St. area, where the shooting occurred, is safe and full of decent people.
Bellon used to operate Croma Electronics in the front of his home, but neighbours say he had recently received psychiatric treatment and had been behaving erratically.
Harris said she was in the back of her clinic with a patient when she heard Bellon banging on her locked front door.
"He hardly spoke, actually. I think it was just his rage," Harris said in an interview at her clinic yesterday.
Harris said she didn't immediately call police.

"As soon as I had a break with my work here I wanted to go next door to him and talk to him and see if I could help him in any way," she said. "Perhaps in hindsight maybe it's just as well I called the police. He would have turned that anger towards me. That's what I feel."
She called 911 about 3 p.m. and police came about three hours later. "It might have been my fault that they came so late," she said.
"Because when I called 911 I told them ... this was just a man maybe who needed help and who the police could just talk to."
After police arrived, she stayed in her clinic, later hearing shots that she thought were just from a car backfiring.
When she heard what happened, "I was very distraught."
